name: Uma Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Uma. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not tied to companies, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the robot welding cell at Harrow Agri. We build farm machinery, trailers, muck spreaders, bale handlers, and my cell welds the chassis, the big steel frames underneath. There are two welding robots and a turntable, and I've got two lads who load the jigs and do the hand welds the robots can't reach. I start at seven, check the wire and the gas, run the first frame, and spend the day tweaking robot paths when the steel comes in a bit off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like teaching the robot. When a new frame design comes in, I'm the one who programs the weld paths, and when the first one comes out clean I feel like I've built it with my own hands. What wears me out is that the pay doesn't match. I do the programming the engineers used to do and I'm on operator money. My husband Sean works on his dad's dairy farm, we rent the cottage from his dad cheap, and we still only have a couple of weeks put by after last year's wedding.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to check robot code, to work out weld settings for new steel, to plan meals, even to help Sean's dad with his milk records. Some of the lads at church think it's a bit much. I think it's a tool, like a good welder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. I'd be a bit surprised, honestly, because it already helps me every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people expected too much from it. Same as any tool, it's as good as the person using it. I'd say that at work and probably at Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for me. I'd still be the one programming the robots, still on operator pay. The tools save me an hour or two a week, which I'd keep using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd ask Harrow to put me on the engineering technician grade, because I'm doing the work already, and I'd show them the weld programs I've written. And I'd keep using AI for the weld settings, because it gets me to a good first weld faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any other week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you been put on the technician grade already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've only got a two-year diploma, not the engineering degree. HR goes by paper. My manager says he's on my side, but he's not the one who signs. I'd keep at it, politely, with evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the lads at church think the AI is a bit much. What do they mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They think it's replacing thinking. Some of the older men say a person should know their work without a machine telling them. I understand that. But my grandad used a calculator and nobody said he was cheating.

S0.say: It's a good tool and people expected too much from it. Like any tool, it's as good as the person using it.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me: I'd still program the robots on operator pay. The tools save me an hour or two a week, so I'd keep using them.
S0.do: Keeps working as before and asks Harrow to move her to the engineering technician grade, showing the weld programs she's written. Keeps using AI to reach a good first weld faster.
S0.quote: My grandad used a calculator and nobody said he was cheating.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is a traditional, churchgoing woman who is also the most tech-forward person on her shop floor. Her complaint is credentials: she does engineers' work without the degree HR requires. She sees AI as a tool and defends it gently against older men at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady change. That's my world already, honestly. I'm the robot person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for people who are willing to learn. Firms have to compete, and the ones that use it well will win the orders. I'd also say the firms should train their own people instead of hiring strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. More robots means more need for someone who can set them up, and I already do that. I'd feel for the lads in my cell, though, because the hand welds and loading would go to a third robot soon enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the production manager with a proposal for a third robot cell with me running both, and ask for the technician grade as part of it. I'd do the offline programming certificate, where you plan robot paths on a computer without stopping the line, in the evenings. And I'd use AI to help write the proposal and check the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like starting a new frame design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel for the lads in your cell. What would you do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach them what I know. Kyle's sharp, he could run a cell in a year if he'd stop being on his phone. Danny's not interested, he wants to do farm work anyway. I can't make people learn, but I can open the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're proposing a robot that might replace them. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits all right, if I'm honest. If Harrow doesn't do it, the big machinery makers will, and then we all go. Better a smaller team in a firm that survives. That's how my dad saw it on the farm when he bought the milking robot.

S1.say: It's good for people willing to learn, and firms that use it well will win the orders. Firms should train their own people instead of hiring strangers.
S1.think: More robots means more need for someone to set them up, which I already do. The hand welds and loading in my cell would go to a third robot soon enough.
S1.do: Proposes a third robot cell to the production manager, with her running both and moving to technician grade. Takes an evening certificate in offline robot programming and uses AI to write the proposal and check the numbers.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, like starting a new frame design.
S1.quote: Better a smaller team in a firm that survives.
S1.fieldNote: Uma would actively bring in the robot that shrinks her own team, and she defends that with a free-market view that firms must compete. She still feels responsible for her two helpers and would train the one who wants to learn. Her father's milking robot is her model for how change should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. With robots doing everything hands-on. So even setting up the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should hold on to what matters: family, faith, community, work where we can find it. And I'd say the government shouldn't just pay everyone to sit at home, because people need purpose. That's my honest view, even in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one rattles me. If the AI can program the weld paths better than me, I'm a year or two ahead of everyone, and then I'm not. We've got two weeks of savings and Sean's farm barely breaks even. Being early to new things only helps if there's somewhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could, cancel the car upgrade, and we'd cut our spending to the bone. I'd start doing weld repairs for farmers on Saturdays, out of Sean's dad's shed, because farmers always need a broken gate or trailer hitch fixed today. And I'd learn every new AI and robot system as it comes out, so I'm the last person they let go, not the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it a lot. But I'd be doing things, not sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want people paid to sit at home. If you lost the job, what would you live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm, at first. Family. Weld repairs. I'd take help if I truly had to, I'm not proud about food on the table. But I'd want it tied to work of some kind, even community work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sean say, sitting at the kitchen table that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we've got the cows and the cottage and each other. That's Sean. He's calmer than me. Then he'd ask if I can fix the slurry pump, because it's been leaking for a month.

S2.say: We should hold on to family, faith, community and work where we can find it. The government shouldn't just pay everyone to sit at home, because people need purpose.
S2.think: If AI programs weld paths better than me, my head start lasts a year or two. With two weeks of savings and a farm that barely breaks even, being early only helps if there's somewhere to go.
S2.do: Saves everything, cancels the car upgrade and cuts spending to the bone. Starts Saturday weld repairs for farmers from her father-in-law's shed and keeps learning every new AI and robot system to be the last let go.
S2.feel: Anxious and praying a lot, but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: Being early to new things only helps if there's somewhere to go.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI takes away Uma's main advantage, being ahead with robots, and she knows it. She turns to family, the farm and small repair work, and accepts public help only if tied to work. Her husband Sean is the calm one, and the leaking slurry pump showed how ordinary life would carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's enough to get a few things in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use the time well. Learn, save, build something, look after each other. And I'd say firms should train their own people now while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means three or four good years for someone like me. I'd be the robot person at Harrow while they automate, and I'd use that time to build something on the side that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the offline programming certificate and push hard for the technician grade, because that's real money for a few years. I'd start the farm weld repairs properly, with a sign at the farm gate and a page online. And we'd save at least a quarter of the extra pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. But mostly like I've got a plan, and that settles me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does a repair business feel safer than the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's local and it's about trust. A farmer with a broken hitch at harvest wants someone he knows, today, not a robot booked for Thursday. It might not last forever. But it'll last longer than a job a company can switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the five years change your plans for family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for a baby in a couple of years. Five years is long enough to live your life. I'd just want the repair work going first, so I can work from the farm when the baby comes.

S3.say: Use the time well: learn, save, build something and look after each other. Firms should train their own people now while there's time.
S3.think: Five years means three or four good years as the robot person at Harrow while they automate. I'd use that time to build something on the side that's mine.
S3.do: Takes the offline programming certificate and pushes for technician grade, then launches farm weld repairs properly with a sign at the gate and a web page. Saves at least a quarter of the extra pay.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, but settled by having a plan.
S3.quote: A farmer with a broken hitch at harvest wants someone he knows, today, not a robot booked for Thursday.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Uma combine a few well-paid factory years with a repair business built on local trust. She admits the business may not last forever but expects it to outlast a factory job. Family plans, a baby in a couple of years, stay on track in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a good long stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Train up, save, start something, raise your family well. And don't wait for someone else to sort it out for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of most of it. I'd ride the automation at Harrow, then go out on my own. By the end, I'd want to be the one who owns the robots, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First couple of years, the certificate and the technician grade. Then I'd start the repair business, and around year four or five I'd take out a loan for a second-hand welding robot and do small batch fabrication for local farms, gates, feeders, trailer parts. I'd leave Harrow when the business pays as much. And I'd use AI for everything on the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Hopeful. Ten years is long enough to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan for a robot with thin savings. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I wouldn't do it until the repairs were paying steadily for a couple of years. My father-in-law borrowed for the milking robot and everyone said he was mad. Now he gets to sleep past five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point as the two-year picture. Why calm now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be the one holding the controls when it arrives. With two years, it happens to me. With ten, I get to be ready. And whatever happens, I believe we'll be looked after. That's my faith, not a plan, but it helps.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so use it to train up, save, start something and raise your family well. Don't wait for someone else to sort it out for you.
S4.think: I'd probably do well out of most of the decade, riding automation at Harrow and then going out on my own. By the end I want to own the robots, not be replaced by them.
S4.do: Gets the certificate and technician grade, then starts the repair business and around year four or five borrows for a second-hand welding robot to do small batch fabrication for local farms. Leaves Harrow once the business pays as much and uses AI for the business side.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with time to build something real.
S4.quote: By the end, I'd want to be the one who owns the robots, not the one they replace.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Uma plans to move from operating robots to owning one, with a clear condition before she borrows. Her calm comes partly from time and partly from her faith, which she separated clearly from her plan. Her father-in-law's milking robot is again the example she trusts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My head start disappears in a year, we've only got a couple of weeks saved, and the farm can't carry us. What would help is firms having to train their own people, and some help for small rural businesses to get started, loans or grants tied to work, not just money for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the countryside. Everyone pictures robots in cities and big factories. Out here, a broken trailer at harvest can't wait. I think rural places will need people with skills for longer than anyone expects.

headlineQuote: Out here, a broken trailer at harvest can't wait.
portrait: Uma is a 27-year-old robot welding cell lead at a farm machinery plant who programs the robots herself but is on operator pay because she lacks an engineering degree. She lives cheaply in a cottage on her husband Sean's family dairy farm, has a couple of weeks saved after last year's wedding, and uses AI every day while holding traditional views on faith, family and work. In steady change she'd propose the robot that shrinks her own team, but fast AGI makes her anxious because her head start disappears. With five or ten years she plans farm weld repairs and eventually her own welding robot, saying she wants to own the robots rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her head start would vanish within a year and neither their savings nor the farm could carry them.
whatWouldHelp: Firms being required to train their own people, and loans or grants tied to work that help small rural businesses get started.
